newsitem.title: LEBANON: Shi'ite radicals plan Lebanon "hunger revolt".
newsitem.headline: Shi'ite radicals plan Lebanon "hunger revolt".

text.p: Supporters of a radical Shi'ite cleric threatening to mount a civil disobedience campaign against the Beirut government brushed aside an official warning on Thursday and said their "hunger revolt" would go ahead.

Supporters of Sheikh Sobhi Tufaili, a former head of the pro-Iranian Hizbollah (Party of God), dismissed a charge by President Elias Hrawi that they were arming and threatened Lebanon with a return to chaos and lawlessness.
Hrawi said legal measures would be taken against those responsible.
But in a statement faxed to an international news agency in Beirut, a "Preparatory Committee for the Revolt of the Hungry" said the action planned by Tufaili for July 4 would go ahead.
"Mr President, the world will see on July 4 who preserves civil peace, the country's security and and the rights of the hungry," it said.

Tufaili has called on his supporters to gather on July 4 in Baalbek in the eastern Bekaa valley for a march on Beirut and a civil disobedience campaign unless authorities act by then to help the poor in the predominantly Shi'ite Moslem region.
Information Minister Bassem al-Sabaa said Hrawi told a cabinet meeting on Wednesday that security agencies had detected a flow of weapons to "known forces" in the Bekaa.
"It is not acceptable that anyone calls for resisting the government by threatening all kinds of lawlessness practised years ago," Sabaa quoted Hrawi as saying.
Tufaili's supporters denied the weapons charges and said their campaign would be peaceful.
"How could the president's security see weapons which do not exist being brought secretly to the Bekaa and not see our childrens' hunger and humiliation?" the preparatory committee said.
Tufaili says people in the Bekaa are desperately hungry. He has demanded free schooling and hospital treatment, reduction of income tax and exemption from electricity and water bills for the poor.
Tufaili led Hizbollah in the 1980s but no longer holds any post in the movement. He has long been linked in the Arab media to Iranian hardliners and has called the present Hizbollah leaders too soft.

The Bekaa valley, which is controlled by Syrian troops, has suffered economically from a crackdown on illegal drug crops which flourished during the civil war. Residents complain the government has failed to support profitable alternative crops.
